title: Larger-than-memory data
summary: Query five years of trips without loading every row. Compare CSV and Parquet, let DuckDB read the files needed, collect the answer, and write Parquet files.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse), library(duckplyr)

runs.purpose: load duckplyr, which runs dplyr code in the DuckDB database engine

steps.explain: duckplyr runs dplyr verbs in DuckDB, a database engine inside R that reads files directly. Attaching it says it is overwriting dplyr's methods: from now on, this R session sends data frame work to DuckDB where it can. A new lesson restarts R, which undoes that.

steps.title: Text or columns: CSV and Parquet

runs.purpose: find the size of one year of trips as CSV, in megabytes
runs.task: Find the size of `data/trips.csv` in megabytes: `file.size()` divided by `1e6`.

runs.code:
fs::dir_info("data/archive", recurse = TRUE, glob = "*.parquet") |>
  summarize(files = n(), megabytes = as.numeric(sum(size)) / 1e6)
runs.purpose: count the archive's Parquet files and add up their size
runs.task: List `.parquet` files in `data/archive` and its folders with `fs::dir_info(recurse = TRUE, glob = "*.parquet")`. Count them and add their sizes in megabytes.

steps.explain:
One year of trips as CSV takes {csv_mb} MB. The archive holds every trip since the scheme opened, five years, in {n_files} Parquet files of {parquet_mb} MB in all.

CSV stores text, row after row; Parquet stores each column together, compressed and with its type, so the files are smaller and a program can read just the columns it needs. A dataset can outgrow your computer's memory long before it outgrows its disk.

steps.title: A folder per year: partitions

runs.purpose: list the folders inside the 2025 one

steps.explain:
The archive is partitioned: one folder per year, `year=2021` to `year=2025`, and inside each, one folder per month with its file. The folder names hold values, `year=2025` and `month=7`, so the files don't need those columns.

A question about one year only has to open that year's files; this layout is called Hive partitioning, after the system that made it common.

steps.title: Open without reading: read_parquet_duckdb()

runs.purpose: open every Parquet file in the archive as one table, `archive`, reading year and month from the folder names
runs.task: Open all the archive's files, `"data/archive/**/*.parquet"`, with `read_parquet_duckdb()` and `options = list(hive_partitioning = TRUE)`, and store the result in `archive`.

runs.purpose: count the trips in the archive

steps.explain:
`read_parquet_duckdb()` returned at once, because it read nothing: `archive` is a description of the files, and DuckDB reads from them only when asked for a result. `**` matches folders at any depth, and `hive_partitioning = TRUE` turns the folder names into `year` and `month` columns.

The count ran inside DuckDB, which read only what counting needs, and sent back one number: {n_archive} trips.

steps.title: Read only what's needed: filter() and explain()

runs.task: Keep 2025's trips and count them by `month`.

runs.purpose: show how DuckDB will run that query
runs.task: Add `explain()` to the end of the same pipeline, to see DuckDB's plan.

steps.explain:
The pipeline is ordinary dplyr, but DuckDB runs it. `explain()` shows its plan, read from the bottom up: Read Parquet, with the filter on `year` applied to the files themselves (File Filters), so it scans only the 12 files of 2025 out of {n_files}, and reads only the `month` column from them.

Then it counts by month. Filtering on a partition column is the quickest filter of all, since whole files are skipped.

steps.title: Bring home the answer: collect()

runs.code:
by_year <- archive |>
  summarize(
    trips = n(),
    median_minutes = median(duration_min),
    .by = c(year, member_type)
  ) |>
  arrange(year, member_type) |>
  collect()
alternatives: by_year = archive |> summarize(trips = n(), median_minutes = median(duration_min), .by = c(year, member_type)) |> arrange(year, member_type) |> as_tibble()
runs.purpose: summarise each year's trips by rider type in DuckDB, and bring the small result into R as `by_year`
runs.task: For each `year` and `member_type`, count trips and find median `duration_min`. Sort by `year` and `member_type`, then `collect()` into `by_year`.

runs.code:
ggplot(by_year, aes(x = year, y = trips, fill = member_type)) +
  geom_col()
alternatives: ggplot(by_year, aes(year, trips, fill = member_type)) + geom_col()
runs.purpose: chart the trips per year, by rider type
runs.task: Draw `trips` by `year` from `by_year` as stacked bars filled by `member_type`, with `geom_col()`.

steps.explain:
DuckDB summarised half a million trips into ten rows, and `collect()` brought just those into R's memory, as an ordinary tibble that ggplot2 can draw. duckplyr won't quietly pull a large result into memory: asking for every row of `archive` would stop with a message to use `collect()` on purpose.

Trips grew from {first_year_trips} in 2021, the scheme's first, part year, to {last_year_trips} in 2025.

steps.title: Write partitioned Parquet: compute_parquet()

runs.code:
archive |>
  count(year, month, start_station) |>
  compute_parquet(
    "station-months",
    options = list(partition_by = "year", overwrite = TRUE)
  )
runs.purpose: count each station's trips per month in every year, and write the counts as Parquet, one folder per year
runs.task: Count `archive` by `year`, `month` and `start_station`, and write the result with `compute_parquet()` to `station-months`, with `options = list(partition_by = "year", overwrite = TRUE)`.

steps.explain:
`compute_parquet()` runs the query in DuckDB and writes the result straight to Parquet, without bringing it into R. `partition_by = "year"` makes a `year=` folder for each year, as in the archive, and `overwrite = TRUE` replaces what an earlier run wrote. The Files pane shows `station-months`.

Read and write Parquet with duckplyr, or with arrow, which works the same way, whenever data is too big to read comfortably.
